content.stem: A steel producer's executive team sets a three-year breakthrough objective to cut customer claims by 60%. Annual objectives are negotiated down through mill management, with each level proposing means and feeding constraints back up before plans are locked. This iterative negotiation is best described as:
content.why: The back-and-forth negotiation of targets and means between organizational levels is catchball, the defining communication mechanism of hoshin kanri. MBO sets targets top-down without the iterative means negotiation; scorecard cascading translates metrics but does not require negotiation loops.

options: Probability of completing within four months
Availability of a trained Black Belt to lead it
Existence of baseline data in the historian
content.stem: When selecting Six Sigma projects, the FIRST screening criterion should be:
content.why: Projects are screened first for strategic alignment — a perfectly executed project on an unimportant problem wastes scarce Belt capacity. Resourcing, duration, and data availability are feasibility filters applied after alignment.

options: At least 30 observations per group and blocking
Equal sample sizes, normal x's, random effects
Normal residuals, equal variances across groups, independent observations
content.stem: Key assumptions of one-way ANOVA are:
content.why: ANOVA requires normally distributed residuals, homogeneity of variance, and independence. Equal n is helpful (robustness) but not required. Residual plots and Levene's/Bartlett's tests check these.

content.stem: A 3×4 contingency table tests whether defect type is independent of shift. The chi-square degrees of freedom are:
content.why: df = (r−1)(c−1) = 2 × 3 = 6. Also remember the expected-count guideline (most cells ≥5) and that expected count = (row total × column total)/grand total.

content.stem: In that table, a cell's row total is 60, column total is 40, and the grand total is 200. Its expected count is:
content.why: E = (60 × 40)/200 = 12. The chi-square statistic sums (O−E)²/E across cells; large contributions localize where the association lives.

options: 72% of yield variation is associated with the linear relationship with temperature
85% of yield variation is explained by temperature
content.stem: A correlation of r = 0.85 between reheat furnace temperature and yield strength means:
content.why: Explained variation = r² = 0.85² ≈ 0.72. Correlation is not causation (option C), and r is not the slope — slope depends on the variables' units and spreads.

content.stem: A fitted model is ŷ = 12 + 3.5x (x = %Mn ×10). If x increases by 2 units, predicted y changes by:
content.why: Slope × change = 3.5 × 2 = +7.0. The intercept (12) is the prediction at x = 0 and is often outside the data range — interpreting it physically is a common error the exam probes.

options: H₀: β₁ = 0 — no linear relationship between x and y
content.stem: In simple linear regression output, the p-value on the slope coefficient tests:
content.why: The slope's t-test evaluates H₀: β₁ = 0. A small p-value indicates a statistically detectable linear relationship — but always check residuals and beware extrapolation beyond the fitted range.

content.stem: A residuals-versus-fitted plot shows scatter that fans out as fitted values increase. This indicates:
content.why: A funnel shape is the classic sign of heteroscedasticity, violating the constant-variance assumption. Remedies: transform y (log/sqrt) or use weighted least squares. Autocorrelation shows as patterns versus time/order.

options: Individual coefficient estimates are unstable with inflated standard errors, though overall prediction may remain useful
content.stem: In multiple regression, two predictors (billet temperature and descale water temperature) have VIFs of 14 and 12. The consequence is:
content.why: VIF > ~10 signals serious multicollinearity: correlated predictors make it impossible to separate their individual effects (unstable, sign-flipping coefficients), even while the joint fit predicts adequately. Remedies: drop/combine variables or collect DOE data.

content.stem: A 95% confidence interval for mean wall thickness from n = 64, x̄ = 50, s = 8 is approximately:
content.why: CI = x̄ ± t·s/√n ≈ 50 ± 1.96×(8/8) = 50 ± 1.96 (t≈z at df = 63). Option C wrongly uses s instead of the standard error — the single most common CI error.

options: It will contain 95% of future sample means
The procedure generating such intervals captures µ 95% of the time
95% of individual pipes fall inside it
There is a 95% probability µ is in this specific interval
content.stem: Which statement about that confidence interval is correct?
content.why: The frequentist meaning: the method captures µ in 95% of repeated samples — a specific computed interval either contains µ or doesn't. Intervals for individuals are prediction/tolerance intervals, a distinction ASQ tests.

options: Lean: designing new products; Six Sigma: sustaining existing controls
Lean: eliminating waste and improving flow; Six Sigma: reducing variation in CTQs
Lean: statistical control; Six Sigma: workplace organization
Lean: reducing variation; Six Sigma: reducing lead time
content.stem: Which pairing correctly contrasts the primary emphasis of Lean versus Six Sigma?
content.why: Lean attacks waste and flow (time, inventory, motion); Six Sigma attacks variation and defects in critical-to-quality characteristics. They are complementary, which is why integrated Lean Six Sigma deployments dominate.

content.stem: Historical thread-defect proportion is 5%. A sample of 300 shows 8% defective. Testing H₀: p = 0.05 vs H₁: p > 0.05, the test statistic is approximately:
content.why: z = (0.08−0.05)/√(0.05×0.95/300) = 0.03/0.01258 ≈ 2.39 — reject at α = 0.05 (critical 1.645 one-tailed). Note the standard error uses the hypothesized p₀, and proportions use z, not t.

content.stem: Cycle-time data from two crews are strongly skewed with outliers, n = 9 per crew. The most defensible comparison of central tendency is:
content.why: Small samples + strong skew undermine the t-test's normality reliance — the Mann-Whitney compares two independent groups without assuming normality. Kruskal-Wallis is its ≥3-group extension; Levene's tests variances.

options: Positional (within-piece) variation sources such as roll eccentricity or die alignment
Temporal variation sources such as tool wear
Cyclical (lot-to-lot) variation such as heat chemistry
content.stem: A multi-vari chart of wall thickness shows large variation within a single pipe (around the circumference) that dwarfs pipe-to-pipe and hour-to-hour variation. The team should focus on:
content.why: Multi-vari classifies variation as positional (within-piece), cyclical (piece-to-piece), and temporal (time-to-time). Dominant within-piece variation points to spatial mechanisms — eccentricity, alignment — not time-based drift.

options: Slivers are attribute data, so correlation cannot exist
Correlation from observational data may be confounded — e.g., Supplier B slabs may be rolled disproportionately on one shift or caster strand
The sample must exceed 1,000 pipes for correlation
content.stem: An improvement team observes that pipes made from Supplier B slabs correlate with more slivers, and immediately declares Supplier B the root cause. The strongest methodological objection is:
content.why: Observational associations are vulnerable to confounding/lurking variables; only randomized experimentation (or careful stratified analysis) supports causal claims. This is the core logic gap between Analyze's screening and Improve's DOE.

content.stem: When testing whether observed heat-chemistry failure counts across five furnaces match the proportions expected from tonnage share, the appropriate test is:
content.why: Comparing one set of observed category counts to expected proportions is the chi-square goodness-of-fit test (df = k−1). Independence (contingency) tests instead examine association between two categorical variables.

content.stem: A team studies 3 factors, each at 2 levels, in a full factorial with 2 replicates. The total number of runs is:
content.why: 2³ = 8 treatment combinations × 2 replicates = 16 runs. Replication (repeating full combinations) provides a pure error estimate; repetition (multiple measurements within a run) does not — a tested distinction.

content.stem: In a 2² experiment, responses at factor A high are 52, 58, 60, 66 and at A low are 40, 44, 48, 52. The main effect of A is:
content.why: Effect A = ȳ(A+) − ȳ(A−) = (52+58+60+66)/4 − (40+44+48+52)/4 = 59 − 46 = 13. A main effect is the average response change from low to high level, averaged over all other factors.

content.stem: To screen 4 factors in only 8 runs, the team uses a 2⁴⁻¹ design with generator I = ABCD. This design's resolution is:
content.why: The shortest word in the defining relation has length 4 → Resolution IV: main effects are clear of two-factor interactions, but two-factor interactions alias each other (e.g., AB = CD). Resolution = length of shortest defining word.

options: Main effects are aliased with two-factor interactions
content.stem: The critical weakness of a Resolution III design is that:
content.why: In Resolution III, main effects are confounded with 2-factor interactions — a 'significant' main effect may actually be an interaction. Use Res III only for early screening when interactions are believed negligible, then de-alias with a foldover.

options: Detect curvature in the response surface
content.stem: Adding center points to a 2-level factorial primarily allows the experimenter to:
content.why: Comparing the center-point mean with the factorial-point mean tests for curvature — if significant, the linear (2-level) model is inadequate and an RSM design (e.g., central composite) is warranted. Replicated centers also give pure error.

content.stem: A balanced scorecard is being built for a tubular products division. 'Percentage of heats released within 24 hours of final chemistry' belongs in which perspective?
content.why: Cycle-time and first-pass-yield style metrics measure how well internal processes execute. The customer perspective would capture what the customer experiences (on-time delivery, claims); financial captures outcomes like margin.

options: Randomizing run order and/or blocking on time period
content.stem: Furnace lining degrades slowly over a campaign, and the team fears it will bias a week-long DOE. The correct countermeasure built INTO the design is:
content.why: Randomization converts unknown time trends into noise instead of bias, and blocking removes known nuisance variation (day/campaign period) from the error term. This is the canonical answer for lurking time-based variables.

options: The effect of quench rate depends on the tempering temperature level
The factors are correlated in the design matrix
content.stem: On an interaction plot of quench rate × tempering temperature, strongly non-parallel lines indicate:
content.why: Non-parallel lines are the graphical signature of interaction — one factor's effect changes with the other's level. With strong interactions, interpreting main effects alone is misleading; optimize using the interaction.

options: Repeat the fractional factorial with more replicates
Steepest ascent to the promising region, then a central composite design to model curvature
content.stem: After screening identifies two vital factors, the team wants to locate optimum settings on a curved response surface. The standard sequential strategy is:
content.why: Classic RSM sequence: linear model → path of steepest ascent → detect curvature → CCD/Box-Behnken to fit a second-order model and locate the optimum. OFAT famously misses interaction-driven optima.

options: Requires halting the line for each run
Uses large, deliberate factor changes offline
Makes small factor changes during routine production so output stays saleable while improvement accumulates
content.stem: EVOP (evolutionary operation) differs from a conventional DOE in that it:
content.why: EVOP runs tiny planned perturbations within operating tolerance during normal production, iterating cycles until small effects emerge from noise. Its virtue: continuous improvement without scrap or downtime.

options: Two or more effects cannot be separated because they are estimated by the same contrast
The response could not be measured reliably
content.stem: Confounding in an experiment means:
content.why: Confounded (aliased) effects share an estimation contrast — the data cannot tell them apart. Fractional designs deliberately accept confounding to save runs; the alias structure tells you exactly what you gave up.

content.stem: A kanban loop must cover demand of 100 units/hr with replenishment lead time of 2 hours, a 20% safety factor, and containers of 25 units. The number of kanban cards required is:
content.why: N = D×L×(1+SF)/C = 100×2×1.2/25 = 9.6 → round up to 10 (rounding down risks stockout). Kanban caps WIP — the number of cards is the WIP ceiling in containers.

options: Converting internal setup to external setup
content.stem: During an SMED analysis of a roll change, moving pre-heating of the incoming roll set so it happens while the mill is still running is an example of:
content.why: Internal setup requires the machine stopped; external can be done while running. SMED's biggest lever is converting internal→external — preparation happens off-line, slashing changeover downtime.

options: Standardize, Sort, Set in order, Shine, Sustain
Shine, Sort, Standardize, Set in order, Sustain
Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain
Sort, Shine, Set in order, Sustain, Standardize
content.stem: The correct order of the 5S steps is:
content.why: Sort → Set in order → Shine → Standardize → Sustain (seiri, seiton, seiso, seiketsu, shitsuke). Sustain — auditing and habit — is where most 5S efforts fail, another commonly tested point.

options: Exploit the constraint — squeeze maximum output from it as-is (no lost minutes, quality-checked feed, staggered breaks)
content.stem: Under the theory of constraints, immediately after identifying the bottleneck (the hydrotester), the next step is to:
content.why: TOC's five steps: identify → exploit → subordinate → elevate → repeat. Exploiting (getting the most from existing capacity) precedes spending money to elevate — capital comes only after free improvements are exhausted.

content.stem: A fixture is redesigned so a coupling can only be loaded in the correct orientation; incorrect loading is physically impossible. This is:
content.why: Devices that make error physically impossible are control/prevention poka-yokes — the strongest class. Warning-type devices merely signal; SPC detects statistically; jidoka stops the machine at abnormality.

content.stem: In a SIPOC for a quench-and-temper line, 'austenitizing furnace temperature profile' is best classified as:
content.why: SIPOC lists high-level process steps; the temperature profile characterizes how a process step is executed (a process variable), not a material input supplied to the process or a deliverable of it. Distinguishing inputs (things transformed/consumed) from process parameters is a classic SIPOC subtlety.

options: RPN dropped from 270 to 72; severity typically stays fixed unless the design itself changes
RPN increased, so the action failed
Detection should always be addressed before occurrence
Severity was reduced by the corrective action
content.stem: After implementing FMEA actions, severity 9, occurrence 6, detection 5 became severity 9, occurrence 2, detection 4. Which statement is correct?
content.why: RPN: 9×6×5 = 270 → 9×2×4 = 72. Severity reflects the consequence of the failure mode and changes only with design changes — actions usually attack occurrence (prevention) first, then detection. High-severity items warrant attention regardless of RPN.

options: Delay implementation until the next budget cycle
Verify predicted results, surface unforeseen side effects, and refine the implementation plan at limited risk
content.stem: Before full rollout, the team runs the new descaling parameters on one shift of one mill stand for two weeks. The primary purposes of this pilot are to:
content.why: Pilots test the solution and the rollout mechanics at contained risk — validating effect size, revealing side effects on secondary metrics, and hardening procedures/training before scale-up.

options: IRR is below the hurdle rate
Payback occurs in under one year
The solution adds economic value after accounting for the time value of money (NPV > 0)
content.stem: A cost-benefit analysis discounts a solution's five-year cash flows at the corporate rate and sums them against implementation cost. A positive result means:
content.why: Discounted benefits exceeding discounted costs is exactly NPV > 0, the accept criterion. It implies IRR > hurdle rate and B/C ratio > 1 — the three criteria agree for conventional cash flows.

content.stem: A brainstorming session anchored by the question 'How could we make this defect WORSE?' followed by reversing each answer is:
content.why: Reverse brainstorming exploits how easily people generate failure modes, then inverts them into countermeasures — useful when conventional brainstorming stalls.

options: Is a rapid (typically 3–5 day) full-time team event implementing focused improvements immediately
content.stem: A kaizen blitz differs from a DMAIC project mainly in that a blitz:
content.why: A kaizen event compresses improvement into a short, dedicated, implement-as-you-go burst on a well-bounded problem. DMAIC suits complex/unknown-cause problems needing data over weeks or months.

options: Publishing daily output targets by stand
Adding WIP buffers before the bottleneck
Authorizing upstream production only when a downstream kanban signals consumption
content.stem: Which change most directly converts a push system to a pull system on a finishing floor?
content.why: Pull means downstream consumption authorizes upstream work — kanban is the authorization signal, and WIP is capped by card count. Better forecasts or targets still push material regardless of downstream need.

content.stem: Hydrotest pressure is recorded once per pipe with no rational way to subgroup. The correct control chart is:
content.why: Single measurements per time point → I-MR. Its control limits use the average moving range (MR̄/d₂ with d₂ = 1.128 for MR of 2); it is more sensitive to non-normality than X̄ charts, which benefit from the CLT.

content.stem: A mill charts the COUNT of surface defects per 100 m of inspected pipe, where inspected length varies day to day. The correct chart is:
content.why: Counts of defects with a varying area of opportunity → u chart (defects per unit, with limits that vary with n). A c chart requires constant opportunity; p/np charts track defectIVES (units), not defects.

options: Number of defective pipes in samples of constant size
Proportion defective with varying sample size
content.stem: An np chart is appropriate when tracking:
content.why: np = number of defectives, constant n. If n varies, use the p chart. The defect/defective distinction (Poisson vs binomial basis) drives the entire attribute-chart selection tree.

content.stem: X̄ chart parameters: X̿ = 352, R̄ = 8, n = 5 (A₂ = 0.577). The UCL for the X̄ chart is approximately:
content.why: UCL = X̿ + A₂R̄ = 352 + 0.577×8 = 352 + 4.62 ≈ 356.6. Note these limits bound subgroup MEANS, not individuals — comparing spec limits (for individuals) to X̄ limits is a classic error.

content.stem: A mill's quality costs last year: prevention $20k, appraisal $50k, internal failure $120k, external failure $60k. The cost of poor quality (COPQ) is:
content.why: COPQ = internal + external failure costs = 120k + 60k = $180k. Prevention and appraisal are costs of good quality (conformance). Total cost of quality would be $250k — a distractor testing the COQ/COPQ distinction.

content.stem: A p chart has p̄ = 0.04 with constant subgroups of n = 200. Its UCL is approximately:
content.why: σ_p = √(0.04×0.96/200) = 0.01386; UCL = 0.04 + 3(0.01386) ≈ 0.082. If the LCL computes negative, it is set to zero — another standard follow-up question.

options: Five consecutive points alternating sides of center
Two of three consecutive points beyond 2σ on the same side
content.stem: Under the Western Electric rules, which pattern signals an out-of-control condition even though no point exceeds 3σ?
content.why: 2-of-3 beyond 2σ (same side) is a WE zone rule, as are 4-of-5 beyond 1σ and 8 consecutive on one side. Zone rules increase sensitivity to small shifts at the cost of more false alarms.

content.stem: For detecting a sustained small shift (~0.5σ to 1σ) in a critical chemistry parameter, the most sensitive charts are:
content.why: CUSUM and EWMA accumulate information across points, detecting small sustained shifts far faster than memoryless Shewhart charts, which excel at large abrupt shifts. Many mills run both in parallel.

content.stem: The in-control average run length (ARL₀) of a standard 3σ Shewhart chart — the average points between false alarms — is approximately:
content.why: False-alarm probability per point = 0.0027, so ARL₀ = 1/0.0027 ≈ 370. Adding sensitizing rules lowers ARL₀ (more false alarms) while shortening detection ARL for real shifts — a deliberate trade-off.

options: Capture only common-cause variation within subgroups so special causes appear BETWEEN subgroups
content.stem: Subgroups for an X̄-R chart on wall thickness should be formed from consecutive pipes off one stand rather than mixing stands, because rational subgrouping seeks to:
content.why: Rational subgroups are chosen so within-subgroup variation is pure common cause; assignable causes (stand differences, shift changes) then show up between subgroups where the chart can flag them. Mixing streams inflates R̄, widening limits and hiding signals.

content.stem: A stable process is producing within limits, but an operator adjusts the machine after every measurement that deviates from target. The predictable result, per Deming's funnel experiment, is:
content.why: Adjusting in response to common-cause variation is tampering — funnel rule 2 roughly doubles variance. Control charts exist precisely to distinguish signals worth acting on from noise that must be left alone (or attacked systemically).

content.stem: When subgroup size is 12, the preferred variables chart pair is:
content.why: Above n ≈ 8–10 the range wastes information; X̄-s uses the subgroup standard deviation, a more efficient spread estimator at larger n. R charts persist at small n mainly for shop-floor simplicity.

options: Process step, characteristic, spec/tolerance, measurement method, sample size and frequency, control method, reaction plan
Team roster, budget, and Gantt chart
Only the characteristic and its specification
Histogram, box plot, and run chart
content.stem: Which set of elements must a control plan row contain to be actionable?
content.why: A control plan links each critical characteristic to how it's measured, how often, how it's controlled, and exactly what to do when it goes wrong (reaction plan). Missing reaction plans are the most common audit finding.

options: Stop and call for a full DOE
content.stem: In pre-control, production begins after five consecutive units fall in the green zone. If, during running checks, two consecutive units fall in the SAME yellow zone, the operator should:
content.why: Pre-control rules: two consecutive same-zone yellows → adjust; two opposite yellows or any red → stop and investigate. Pre-control is a simple setup/centering tool, not a substitute for SPC on critical characteristics.

content.stem: In total productive maintenance, routine cleaning, lubrication, and inspection performed by production operators themselves is called:
content.why: Autonomous maintenance transfers routine care to operators, freeing maintenance crews for planned/predictive work and catching deterioration early — a TPM pillar directly aimed at raising OEE availability.

options: Adding a second Charpy machine to cut test backlog
Replacing final pipe inspection with statistical audit sampling
Investing in mill-stand setup capability studies so inspection can be reduced
content.stem: Reclassifying which activity would move cost from appraisal to prevention?
content.why: Prevention spends money to stop defects from occurring (capability studies, planning, training). Options A, C, D all still detect or sort — appraisal. The exam expects you to classify by intent (prevent vs. detect), not by department.

options: Visual controls making status and abnormality immediately obvious
content.stem: Andon lights, shadow boards, and floor-marked kanban squares are examples of:
content.why: Visual factory/controls let anyone judge normal vs abnormal at a glance, shrinking response time to problems. They inform and signal; unlike control-type poka-yokes, they do not physically prevent error.

options: Free the Black Belt for new projects
Institutionalize the gains so performance persists without the project team
content.stem: At project closure, the control plan, updated SOPs, and trained operators are formally transferred to the process owner, and audits are scheduled at 30/90/180 days. The primary purpose is to:
content.why: Control-phase handoff exists to sustain the gains: ownership, documentation, training, monitoring, and audit cadence together prevent regression — the most common post-project failure.

content.stem: After a successful project on Mill 1, the deployment leader documents the solution and drives adoption at two sister mills with similar processes. This practice is:
content.why: Replication multiplies project ROI by transferring proven solutions to similar processes — a formal expectation of mature deployments, usually coordinated through lessons-learned databases and MBB networks.

content.stem: The DMADV road map, in correct order, is:
content.why: Define-Measure-Analyze-Design-Verify is used when no process/product exists or the current one cannot reach entitlement — versus DMAIC, which improves an existing process. Choosing DMAIC vs DMADV is itself a tested judgment.

options: Correlations (supporting or conflicting) among the technical characteristics
content.stem: In the house of quality (QFD), the triangular 'roof' matrix captures:
content.why: The roof shows interactions between the HOWs — where improving one technical characteristic helps or fights another (e.g., wall thickness vs weight). This is where design trade-offs first become visible.

options: Customer needs → technical requirements → part characteristics → process parameters → production controls
content.stem: In multi-phase QFD, the outputs (HOWs) of house 1 become the inputs (WHATs) of house 2. This cascade translates:
content.why: QFD's four linked houses flow customer voice down to shop-floor controls, preserving traceability so every process setting can be traced to a customer need.

content.stem: A designer needs a pipe coating that is both hard (scratch resistance) and flexible (bend without cracking) — a classic physical contradiction. The methodology built specifically to resolve such contradictions without compromise is:
content.why: TRIZ systematizes inventive problem solving around resolving technical/physical contradictions using the 40 inventive principles and separation strategies (in time, space, condition) — instead of trading one requirement off against the other.

content.stem: A team scores five design concepts against weighted criteria relative to a datum concept using +, −, and S, iterating and hybridizing the strongest concepts. This is:
content.why: The Pugh matrix compares concepts against a datum, encouraging hybrid concepts through iteration ('controlled convergence'). It is deliberately coarse — its power is structured comparison, not false numerical precision.

options: Find control-factor settings whose performance is insensitive to noise (robustness)
Reduce the number of experimental runs
Estimate their main effects for control
content.stem: In Taguchi parameter design, noise factors are placed in an outer array PRIMARILY to:
content.why: Noise factors (ambient temperature, incoming material spread) cannot be economically controlled in production — parameter design seeks control-factor settings that minimize sensitivity to them, often via signal-to-noise ratios or control×noise interactions.

content.stem: Taguchi's loss function for a nominal-is-best characteristic is L = k(y − T)². With k = $4,000/mm² and a part produced 0.05 mm from target, the loss per part is:
content.why: L = 4000 × (0.05)² = 4000 × 0.0025 = $10. The quadratic loss model's key message: loss begins the moment you leave target — not at the spec limit — which is the philosophical break from goalpost thinking.

content.stem: A quality director benchmarks the claims-handling process of a top airline rather than another steelmaker. This is:
content.why: Studying an analogous function in an unrelated industry is functional/generic benchmarking. Competitive benchmarking targets direct rivals; internal compares sites within the company; performance benchmarking compares metrics without studying the process.

content.stem: Two components stack in an assembly with independent tolerances ±0.03 mm and ±0.04 mm. The statistical (RSS) tolerance of the stack is:
content.why: RSS = √(0.03² + 0.04²) = √0.0025 = ±0.05 mm. Worst-case stacking gives ±0.07 — RSS exploits the improbability of simultaneous extremes, enabling looser (cheaper) component tolerances at a small statistical risk.

content.stem: A design review reduces a housing from 12 parts to 5, eliminates 4 fastener types, and makes remaining parts self-locating. This activity is:
content.why: DFA/DFMA reduces part count, standardizes, and simplifies handling/insertion — cutting assembly cost AND failure opportunities (fewer parts, fewer interfaces, fewer defects).

options: Verification: does the design meet its specifications? Validation: does the product meet user needs in the use environment?
Verification is done by customers; validation by engineers
content.stem: The essential difference between design verification and design validation is:
content.why: Verification = built the product right (conformance to specs, testing/analysis). Validation = built the right product (fulfills intended use under actual/simulated use conditions, ideally with users). Both are required, in that order.

options: Failures caused by manufacturing and assembly variation
Failure modes arising from the product's design characteristics, before drawings are released
content.stem: A design FMEA differs from a process FMEA primarily in that a DFMEA addresses:
content.why: DFMEA targets potential design weaknesses (material choice, geometry, tolerancing) early — when change is cheap; PFMEA targets how manufacturing can fail to build the design correctly. Timing is the point: FMEA value collapses if done after decisions are frozen.

content.stem: A subsystem has three components in series with reliabilities 0.95, 0.98, and 0.99. System reliability is approximately:
content.why: Series reliability multiplies: 0.95 × 0.98 × 0.99 ≈ 0.922 — always below the weakest component. Improving series reliability requires better components or adding parallel redundancy around the weak link.

content.stem: Early in concept design, a team allocates the system-level CTQ 'coating adhesion ≥ X' down into measurable requirements on surface prep, primer chemistry, and cure profile, each with its own target and tolerance. This activity is called:
content.why: CTQ flow-down decomposes system requirements into subsystem and component requirements with allocated targets/variances, so capability can be predicted bottom-up (flow-up) before hardware exists — a core DFSS discipline.

options: Validate the measurement system before Analyze
Approve the project charter and tollgates
Fund the project and remove barriers
Sustain and continuously manage the process after handoff
content.stem: The process owner's distinct responsibility, as opposed to the project sponsor's, is to:
content.why: The process owner lives with the process day-to-day and owns the control plan after project closure. Funding, barrier removal, and tollgate approval are sponsor duties; MSA execution belongs to the team.

content.stem: 'Number of overdue preventive-maintenance work orders on the stretch reducer' is being tracked to predict future delay minutes. This metric is best described as a:
content.why: It measures an upstream condition expected to predict future performance (delays), making it a leading indicator. Delay minutes themselves would be the lagging result measure.

options: Shipping-status inquiries answered within one business hour
Implement a new ERP tracking module
content.stem: A customer says: 'Your pipe is fine but I can never reach anyone about shipping status.' The correct translation into a CTQ is:
content.why: A CTQ must be a measurable characteristic of the output with a performance target — 'answered within one business hour' is specific and measurable. Options A and D are solutions; C is too vague to measure a requirement.

content.stem: A Black Belt is asked to justify a project portfolio. Project A: initial cost $240,000, uniform net savings $80,000/yr. Ignoring the time value of money, the payback period is:
content.why: Payback = investment ÷ annual net savings = 240,000 / 80,000 = 3.0 years. Payback ignores discounting and post-payback cash flows — a common exam trap is offering NPV-style logic when the stem says to ignore time value.

content.stem: A finishing floor holds an average of 480 pipes as WIP and completes 120 pipes per hour. By Little's law, the average time a pipe spends in finishing is:
content.why: Little's law: CT = WIP / throughput = 480 / 120 = 4 hours. Watch the arrangement — WIP = TH × CT is the same law; the exam frequently asks you to solve for a different variable.

options: Manage closely with weekly working sessions
Keep informed through detailed technical reports
Monitor only, with no proactive communication
Keep satisfied with concise periodic updates
content.stem: Which stakeholder-analysis action is appropriate for a group assessed as high power / low interest in a project's outcome?
content.why: The power/interest grid prescribes keep satisfied for high-power, low-interest stakeholders — enough engagement to avoid surprise opposition without burdening them. 'Manage closely' is reserved for high power / high interest.

content.stem: A division reports first-pass yield per operation: rolling 96%, UT inspection 92%, hydrotest 90%. Rolled throughput yield for the sequence is approximately:
content.why: RTY = product of step yields = 0.96 × 0.92 × 0.90 = 0.795 ≈ 79.5%. RTY exposes the 'hidden factory' — the arithmetic mean (92.7%) is the classic distractor.

content.stem: Three weeks into a project, team members openly challenge the Black Belt's data collection plan, argue over roles, and two subgroups form around competing solutions. Per Tuckman's model, the team is in:
content.why: Conflict over roles, authority, and approach is the signature of storming. The correct leader response is to facilitate ground rules and channel conflict onto ideas — suppressing it typically pushes the team backward, not forward.

content.stem: A team quickly agrees with the senior metallurgist's diagnosis without examining alternatives; a junior engineer privately doubts it but stays silent to preserve harmony. This dynamic is:
content.why: Suppressing dissent to protect cohesion is groupthink. Consensus requires that alternatives be genuinely examined and every member can support the outcome. A standing devil's-advocate role is one documented countermeasure.

options: Consulted parties must be two-way communicators
Accountable and Responsible may never be the same person
Every task must have at least one R
Only one person may be Accountable per deliverable
content.stem: In a RACI matrix, which rule is violated if the hydrotest supervisor and the quality manager are both listed as 'A' for the same deliverable?
content.why: RACI permits many R's, C's, and I's, but exactly one A per deliverable — split accountability means no accountability. A and R residing in the same person is allowed and common.

content.stem: Under the Thomas-Kilmann conflict model, a Black Belt who works with two engineers to jointly redefine the problem until a solution satisfies both parties' underlying interests is using:
content.why: Collaborating seeks a win-win by addressing underlying interests — highest effort, best for important issues needing buy-in. Compromise splits the difference (both give something up); forcing wins at the other's expense.

options: Avoiding, because the issue is trivial and timing is poor
Compromising, to give each a partial win
content.stem: A conflict between two operators over a trivial workstation preference erupts the day before a critical tollgate. The most appropriate immediate conflict mode is:
content.why: Avoiding is legitimately correct when the issue is trivial, emotions are high, or timing is wrong. The exam tests that no conflict mode is universally right — mode selection depends on issue importance and urgency.

content.stem: After silent idea generation, each member states one idea in rotation, ideas are clarified without criticism, then ranked by private ballot. This technique is:
content.why: Structured rotation plus private ranking defines NGT — it equalizes airtime and neutralizes dominant personalities. Delphi uses anonymous iterative questionnaires with geographically separated experts; classic brainstorming is unstructured and verbal.

options: End the meeting and reschedule with ground rules
Impose round-robin input and directly invite quieter members
Publicly point out the manager is dominating
Privately ask the manager to leave the team
content.stem: A facilitator notices one manager answers most questions and junior members have stopped contributing. The best FIRST intervention is to:
content.why: Structural facilitation techniques — round-robin, directed questions, silent writing — rebalance participation without confrontation. Removal or public criticism are escalations reserved for persistent problems.

options: X is acceptable; Y destroys value at the hurdle rate
Y is acceptable because IRR is within 1% of the hurdle rate
Both are acceptable since both produce positive returns
Neither can be evaluated without payback period
content.stem: Two candidate projects have identical costs. Project X has NPV = +$95,000 at the corporate hurdle rate; Project Y has IRR = 14% versus a hurdle rate of 15%. Which statement is correct?
content.why: A positive NPV at the hurdle rate means X creates value. An IRR below the hurdle rate means Y's return is less than the cost of capital — its NPV at 15% is negative, so it destroys value. Proximity to the hurdle rate is irrelevant to the accept/reject decision.

options: Reach a final binding decision on the root cause
Reduce a long brainstormed list to a manageable few for further analysis
content.stem: Multivoting is most appropriate when a team needs to:
content.why: Multivoting narrows a large list; it is explicitly not a final-decision tool because it can mask strong minority objections. Final selection should use consensus or a criteria-based matrix.

content.stem: Per Herzberg, improving which factor prevents dissatisfaction but does NOT by itself motivate higher performance?
content.why: Pay, conditions, policies, and supervision are hygiene factors — their absence dissatisfies, but their presence does not motivate. Motivators are intrinsic: achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth.

options: Team size above the effective range for working teams
content.stem: A team of eleven struggles to schedule meetings and members disengage during discussions. The MOST likely structural cause is:
content.why: Working project teams are most effective around 5–9 members; beyond that, coordination costs rise and social loafing appears. Large stakeholder groups belong in communication plans, not on the core team.

options: Scheduling all meetings in headquarters time
Relying on email to create a written record
Establishing explicit communication norms and rotating meeting times
content.stem: For a virtual team spanning three time zones, the highest-leverage practice is:
content.why: Virtual teams fail on unmanaged communication: explicit norms (channels, response times, decision rules) and equitable meeting rotation are the documented countermeasures. Email-only starves teams of rich interaction.

content.stem: Six months after training, a company measures whether SPC-trained technicians actually apply control-chart interpretation on the floor. In Kirkpatrick's model this is evaluation at level:
content.why: On-the-job application is Level 3, Behavior. Level 2 is knowledge/skill measured at training (tests); Level 4 is business results (e.g., reduced scrap attributable to the training).

content.stem: A team member repeatedly summarizes discussion, tests for agreement, and draws out silent members. In group-role terms this person is performing:
content.why: Harmonizing, encouraging, gatekeeping (balancing participation), and consensus-testing are maintenance roles that keep the group functioning. Task roles push content (initiating, information-seeking); self-oriented roles serve personal agendas.

options: A formal HR process; mentoring is statistical guidance
Task/skill-specific and performance-focused; mentoring is longer-term and developmental
Only performed by the direct supervisor
Long-term and career-focused; mentoring is task-specific
content.stem: The key distinction between coaching and mentoring a Green Belt is that coaching is:
content.why: Coaching targets specific skills and near-term performance; mentoring is a longer-term developmental relationship covering career and judgment. The MBB typically does both, in different conversations.

options: Individual bonuses tied to whose improvement idea is adopted
content.stem: Which reward practice is MOST likely to damage team performance on a Six Sigma project?
content.why: Rewarding individuals for 'winning' ideas creates internal competition and idea-hoarding, directly undermining collaborative problem solving. Team-level recognition aligned to shared goals is the recommended pattern.

options: Accept the additions to preserve sponsorship
Escalate to the deployment champion immediately
Let the team vote on which metrics to keep
Facilitate a scoping discussion linking each metric to the problem statement and park the rest
content.stem: During Define, the sponsor keeps adding pet metrics to the charter while the team silently complies. The Black Belt's best response is to:
content.why: The Belt's duty is to protect scope through structured facilitation — tie every metric to the problem/goal, use a parking lot for the rest, and document in the charter. Escalation comes only after direct facilitation fails.

options: Recognize contributions, capture lessons learned, and formally close
Extend the project to maintain team cohesion
Immediately reassign members to new projects
content.stem: A team has finished its control plan handoff and validated results. Members feel both pride and loss as assignments end. The leader's most important task in this adjourning stage is to:
content.why: Adjourning requires deliberate closure: recognition, lessons learned, celebration, and formal disbanding. Skipping it wastes organizational learning and demotivates members for future teams.

content.stem: During a Six Sigma deployment, the person who owns barrier removal, secures project resources, and is typically a senior manager with direct stake in the project's business results is the:
content.why: The champion/sponsor removes organizational barriers and secures resources. The MBB provides technical mentorship; the process owner receives the improved process and sustains gains; the steering committee governs the portfolio, not individual project barriers.

options: Acknowledge the history, explore what failed, and involve the operator in piloting the new method
Provide statistical evidence the new method is superior
Cite the sponsor's authority for the change
Reassign the operator away from the pilot line
content.stem: An operator resists a new standard work procedure saying 'we tried something like this in 2019 and it failed.' The most effective influence approach is to:
content.why: Resistance rooted in experience responds to participation and acknowledgment, not authority or data alone — involvement converts a resister into a co-designer. This mirrors the classic change-management finding that participation reduces resistance most durably.

options: Hydrotest first-pass failure rate averaged 6.2% over the last 12 months versus a 2% target, costing $410k in rework
Reduce hydrotest failures by installing automated fill-rate control by Q3
Hydrotest failures are too high because operators skip the fill-rate standard
Hydrotest performance must improve to satisfy our largest customer
content.stem: Which problem statement is correctly written for a project charter?
content.why: A proper problem statement is specific, measured, baselined, bounded in time, and quantified in impact — with no cause and no solution. Option A embeds a cause, B embeds a solution, D is unmeasured.

content.stem: A project network has activities on two paths: A→B→D (5+7+4 days) and A→C→D (5+6+4 days). The critical path duration is:
content.why: Path A-B-D = 5+7+4 = 16 days; A-C-D = 15 days. The critical path is the longest path — it sets minimum project duration. Summing all activities (31) double-counts shared activities.

content.stem: In the activity network diagram below, path A-B is the critical path (6 + 10 = 16 days) and path C-D runs in parallel (9 + 6 = 15 days). The total float (slack) of activity C is:
content.why: Float = critical path length − noncritical path length through that activity = 16 − 15 = 1 day. Activity C can slip one day without delaying the project; activities on the critical path have zero float.

content.stem: In the Kano model, flawless surface finish that customers never mention but whose absence triggers immediate complaints is a:
content.why: Must-be attributes are assumed: fulfilling them earns no credit, missing them causes strong dissatisfaction. Performance attributes scale satisfaction linearly; delighters surprise. Note delighters decay into must-bes over time — a favorite exam nuance.

options: Direct observation of the product in use (going to the gemba)
content.stem: Which VOC collection method is BEST for discovering latent needs customers cannot articulate?
content.why: Observation in the use environment reveals workarounds and unspoken needs — customers can't report what they don't consciously notice. Surveys and focus groups capture only articulated needs; claims data captures only failures.

content.stem: A team collects 120 scattered VOC statements and must organize them into natural need themes before building a CTQ tree. The correct tool is:
content.why: The affinity diagram groups large volumes of verbal data into themes via intuitive silent sorting. The interrelationship digraph comes after, to map cause-effect logic among themes; matrices come later still for prioritization.

content.stem: In a CTQ tree, the correct progression is:
content.why: CTQ trees decompose a general customer need into drivers, then into specific, measurable CTQ requirements with targets/limits. Each level must remain traceable to the original voice of the customer.

options: Detect whether gains are achieved by degrading another output (a consequential/secondary metric)
Satisfy the finance department's reporting needs
Provide a stretch goal for the team
Replace the primary metric if it stalls
content.stem: A project to reduce weld-seam defects tracks 'defects per 100 joints' as the primary metric. The team should ALSO track 'inspection cycle time' primarily to:
content.why: Secondary (consequential) metrics guard against improving the primary metric at the expense of something else — e.g., slowing inspection to catch more defects. This balance requirement appears throughout the BOK.

content.stem: The sponsor asks the team to also fix a labeling problem discovered mid-project because 'you're already in that area.' Accepting without charter revision is an example of:
content.why: Uncontrolled expansion of project boundaries is scope creep — the top killer of project timelines. Legitimate additions go through formal charter change control. Crashing and fast-tracking are schedule-compression techniques.

options: Trains and mentors Belts and shapes deployment strategy
Has authority to approve capital expenditures
Leads more projects simultaneously to increase savings
Reports directly to the CEO in all deployments
content.stem: A Master Black Belt's role differs from a Black Belt's primarily in that the MBB:
content.why: The MBB is the technical and pedagogical leader: training, mentoring, methodology governance, and deployment strategy. Leading many projects personally is a Black Belt pattern; capital authority and reporting lines vary by organization and are not defining.

options: Does not explicitly show task dependencies and the critical path
Only applies to projects over one year
Cannot be updated during the project
content.stem: A Gantt chart's principal limitation compared with a CPM network is that a Gantt chart:
content.why: Gantt charts excel at communicating schedule visually but traditional forms hide dependency logic and float. CPM/PERT networks expose which activities control project duration.

options: Can be assigned, estimated, and tracked as a discrete work package
Maps to one team member's job description
content.stem: A work breakdown structure (WBS) decomposes the project until each element:
content.why: Decomposition stops at work packages — units small enough to assign ownership, estimate cost/duration, and monitor. Over-decomposition adds administrative burden without control benefit.

options: Verify deliverables and decide go / no-go / recycle before committing further resources
Train the team on the next phase's tools
content.stem: The MAIN purpose of a tollgate (phase-gate) review is to:
content.why: Tollgates are governance checkpoints: the sponsor verifies phase deliverables and makes an explicit continue/kill/redirect decision. They protect the organization from sunk-cost momentum.

options: Why this problem matters now — strategic and financial consequence of inaction
The list of in-scope and out-of-scope process steps
Baseline defect rate and measurement period
content.stem: Which element belongs in a project charter's business case rather than its problem statement?
content.why: The business case answers 'why this, why now' — linking the problem to strategy and quantifying the cost of doing nothing. Baseline data belongs to the problem statement; scope and team are separate charter sections.

content.stem: A team defines its project boundary as 'from slab charge into the reheat furnace to first UT inspection.' This charter element is the:
content.why: Start/stop process boundaries define scope. Well-written scope names what is in AND out, preventing later disputes. Goals state targeted improvement magnitude and timing (SMART).

options: Measurable over a sustained, defined condition
content.stem: A goal statement reads: 'Reduce Grade X52 retest rate from 8% to 4% by December 31, verified over 90 days of production.' Which SMART element is MOST clearly demonstrated by the 90-day verification clause?
content.why: The verification window makes the goal measurable under defined, sustained conditions — preventing declaring victory on a lucky short run. It also foreshadows the Control-phase requirement to demonstrate stability.

content.stem: Charpy impact energy in joules, hardness bins of 'soft / target / hard', and heat identification numbers are, respectively:
content.why: Joules have a true zero → ratio. Soft/target/hard is ordered categories → ordinal. Heat IDs are labels with no order → nominal. Data type dictates which statistics and charts are valid — a recurring exam theme.

content.stem: Before collecting hardness data, the team writes: 'Surface hardness = average of three HRB readings taken 90° apart at mid-length on descaled surface, using calibrated tester #7, recorded to 0.1 HRB.' This is a(n):
content.why: An operational definition specifies exactly how a characteristic is measured so different people get consistent values — the prerequisite for meaningful data. It differs from a sampling plan (which/how many units) and calibration (instrument maintenance).

content.stem: To estimate mean coil weight, an analyst numbers all 2,400 coils produced this month and uses a random-number generator to pick 60. Separately, a colleague samples every 40th coil off the line. These schemes are, respectively:
content.why: Equal-probability selection from a full frame = simple random; fixed-interval selection = systematic. Systematic sampling is efficient but dangerous if the interval aligns with a process cycle (e.g., every 40th coil hits the same mandrel position).

content.stem: Yield strength varies by grade, so an analyst samples proportionally within each grade before combining estimates. This is:
content.why: Dividing the population into homogeneous strata and sampling within each reduces estimate variance when strata differ. Cluster sampling instead randomly selects whole groups (e.g., entire heats) and measures everything within them — cheaper, but higher variance.

options: Weakness, because it is an internal limitation
Threat, because it risks future orders
Opportunity, because it justifies capital investment
content.stem: In a SWOT analysis for a pipe mill, 'aging Level-2 automation that limits recipe control' should be classified as a:
content.why: Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external. Aging internal automation is a weakness. The chance to modernize could later be framed as a strategy, but SWOT classification follows the internal/external rule first.

content.stem: A population of tensile results has σ = 12 MPa. For random samples of n = 36, the standard deviation of the sample mean (standard error) is:
content.why: By the central limit theorem, σ_x̄ = σ/√n = 12/√36 = 2 MPa. The CLT also says the distribution of x̄ approaches normal regardless of the parent shape — the basis for control-chart and CI math.

content.stem: A distribution of coating thickness has mean 84 µm, median 78 µm, and a long tail of high values. The distribution is:
content.why: Mean pulled above the median by a high-value tail indicates positive (right) skew. For skewed data, the median is the better center measure and normal-based capability indices become misleading.

content.stem: Defects on pipe coating occur randomly and independently at an average of 2 per pipe. The probability a randomly selected pipe has ZERO coating defects is approximately:
content.why: Poisson: P(0) = e^{−λ} = e^{−2} ≈ 0.135. Poisson applies to counts of independent events over a fixed area/interval; 0.368 (e^{−1}) is the λ=1 trap.

content.stem: Historical data show 5% of couplings fail thread gauging. In a random sample of 10 couplings, the probability that EXACTLY one fails is approximately:
content.why: Binomial: P(1) = C(10,1)(0.05)(0.95)^9 = 10 × 0.05 × 0.630 = 0.315. Requirements: fixed n, constant p, independent trials, binary outcome. 0.599 is P(0) — the classic adjacent trap.

options: Geometric, because we await the first defective
Hypergeometric, because sampling is without replacement from a small finite lot
content.stem: An inspector draws 5 pipes without replacement from an isolated lot of 20, of which 4 are defective. The correct distribution for the number of defectives in the sample is:
content.why: Sampling without replacement from a small finite population changes p on each draw, violating binomial independence — use the hypergeometric. Rule of thumb: binomial approximates well only when n ≤ ~10% of the lot.

content.stem: Yield strength ~ N(500, 20²) MPa. The value that only 5% of heats will exceed is approximately:
content.why: Upper 5% point: 500 + z₀.₉₅σ = 500 + 1.645(20) = 532.9 MPa. Using 1.96 (two-sided value) gives 539.2 — the most common wrong answer. One-sided vs two-sided z is a guaranteed exam trap.

content.stem: For a normal process, the proportion of output falling within ±1.5σ of the mean is approximately:
content.why: P(−1.5 ≤ Z ≤ 1.5) = 2Φ(1.5) − 1 = 2(0.9332) − 1 = 0.8664. Memorize Φ at 1, 1.5, 1.645, 1.96, 2, 2.5, 3 — the exam expects fluent use of the standard normal table.

content.stem: Two independent inspection stations each catch a given defect with probability 0.90. The probability a defective pipe escapes BOTH stations is:
content.why: Escape = miss₁ × miss₂ = 0.10 × 0.10 = 0.01 (independence → multiply). Note 0.19 is the probability of escaping at least one station's detection somewhere — read escape questions carefully.

options: Reject normality; consider transformation or a non-normal capability method
Fail to reject normality; the sample is too small
The test is invalid above n = 50
Data are normal; proceed with Cpk
content.stem: An Anderson-Darling normality test on 80 wall-thickness readings returns p = 0.012. At α = 0.05 the correct conclusion is:
content.why: p (0.012) < α (0.05) → reject the null of normality. Standard Cpk assumes normality; options include Box-Cox/Johnson transformation or distribution-fit capability. AD works fine at n = 80.

content.stem: A process has USL = 470, LSL = 350, mean = 430, and short-term σ = 15. Cpk is approximately:
content.why: Cpu = (470−430)/(3×15) = 0.89; Cpl = (430−350)/45 = 1.78; Cpk = min = 0.89. The process spread would allow Cp = 120/90 = 1.33, but off-center location makes Cpk far worse — the Cp/Cpk gap quantifies centering loss.

content.stem: Under Porter's five forces, a line pipe producer facing customers who can qualify multiple mills to the same API 5L PSL2 requirements is experiencing:
content.why: When buyers can switch among qualified suppliers of an undifferentiated, specification-driven product, buyer power is high. Substitutes would be different product forms (e.g., composite pipe), not alternate suppliers of the same spec.

content.stem: For the same process, Cp = 1.33 while Cpk = 0.89. The single highest-leverage action is to:
content.why: Cp ≫ Cpk means the process is capable but off-center: centering at the spec midpoint (410) would raise Cpk toward 1.33 with no variation reduction needed. Attacking σ first wastes effort.

options: Within-subgroup (short-term) σ, typically from R̄/d₂ or s̄/c₄, while Ppk uses overall long-term σ
The overall standard deviation of all data
Specification width instead of process spread
content.stem: The essential computational difference between Cpk and Ppk is that Cpk uses:
content.why: Cpk = potential/short-term (within-subgroup σ); Ppk = actual/long-term performance (overall σ including between-subgroup drift). A large Cpk−Ppk gap signals instability between subgroups.

content.stem: A process with mean 100 and σ = 4 has a single upper spec at 110. The expected nonconforming rate is approximately:
content.why: Z = (110−100)/4 = 2.5 → tail area ≈ 0.00621 = 6,210 ppm. 1,350 ppm corresponds to Z = 3 and 2,275 ppm to Z = 2 — the exam banks on you knowing these anchors.

content.stem: Inspectors record 45 defects across 500 pipes, each pipe having 3 defect opportunities. DPMO is:
content.why: DPMO = defects / (units × opportunities) × 10⁶ = 45/(500×3) × 10⁶ = 30,000. 90,000 comes from ignoring opportunities (DPU-based ppm) — the distinction between DPU, DPO, and DPMO is heavily tested.

options: A 1.5σ long-term shift of the mean, leaving 4.5σ to the nearer limit
A centered process with ±6σ to each spec limit
content.stem: The statement 'a Six Sigma process produces 3.4 defects per million opportunities' assumes:
content.why: 3.4 ppm is the tail area at Z = 4.5, i.e., a 6σ design allowance minus the conventional 1.5σ long-term shift. A truly centered 6σ process would produce ~0.002 ppm.

options: Marginal (10–30%), acceptable only for some uses
content.stem: A crossed gage R&R study on a tensile machine yields σ_GRR = 0.75 and total observed σ = 2.5 (same units). The %GRR (as % of total variation) indicates the measurement system is:
content.why: %GRR = 0.75/2.5 = 30% — at the unacceptable boundary under the common AIAG guideline (<10% good, 10–30% marginal, >30% unacceptable). The measurement system consumes too much of the observed variation to trust part-to-part conclusions.

content.stem: In the same study, σ_part = 1.2 and σ_GRR = 0.4. The number of distinct categories (ndc) is approximately:
content.why: ndc = 1.41 × (σ_part/σ_GRR) = 1.41 × 3 = 4.23 → 4. Guideline: ndc ≥ 5 for an adequate system; 4 is marginal — the gage can barely distinguish part groups for process analysis.

content.stem: In gage R&R language, variation observed when the SAME operator measures the SAME part repeatedly with the SAME gage is:
content.why: Repeatability = within-operator, equipment variation. Reproducibility = between-operator variation. Mnemonic: repeat = same person repeating; reproduce = another person reproducing the measurement.

content.stem: A gage reads on average 0.8 µm high at the low end of its range and 3.1 µm high at the top end. This pattern is a problem of:
content.why: Bias that changes across the operating range is a linearity error. Constant offset = bias; drift over time = stability; scatter on repeated readings = repeatability.

options: The study needs more parts to compute kappa
Agreement is well below the ~0.75 guideline; inspectors are inconsistent even with themselves
Kappa only applies to variable data
content.stem: An attribute agreement analysis of weld visual inspection returns a within-appraiser kappa of 0.42. The correct interpretation is:
content.why: Kappa corrects agreement for chance; common guidance treats ≥0.75 as good and <0.40 as poor. A within-appraiser kappa of 0.42 means an inspector barely agrees with their own earlier calls — fix operational definitions, standards, and training.

options: Selecting projects smaller than $250,000 in savings
Lack of sustained, visible leadership commitment
Training Green Belts before Black Belts
content.stem: The most frequently cited root cause of failed Six Sigma deployments is:
content.why: Deployment research and ASQ's body of knowledge consistently identify absent or fading leadership commitment as the dominant failure mode — projects stall when sponsors don't remove barriers, free resources, or tie work to strategy.

options: Adequate if two operators average readings
Inadequate: resolution should be ≤ 0.08 mm for this tolerance
content.stem: A caliper with 0.1 mm resolution is proposed for a characteristic with tolerance 0.8 mm. Under the 10:1 (10%) rule, the instrument is:
content.why: The rule of tens: resolution ≤ 1/10 of the tolerance → need ≤0.08 mm. At 0.1 mm the gage rounds away real variation, inflating apparent capability and blinding control charts.

options: Accuracy = calibration interval; precision = gage resolution
Accuracy = small standard deviation; precision = small bias
Accuracy and precision are synonyms in MSA
Accuracy = closeness to the true value; precision = closeness of repeated readings to each other
content.stem: Which pairing correctly distinguishes accuracy from precision?
content.why: Accuracy is location (bias vs. reference standard); precision is spread (repeatability + reproducibility). A gage can be precise but inaccurate — tightly clustered readings all offset from truth.

content.stem: A cell must produce 450 pipes in a 7.5-hour shift (no planned downtime beyond breaks already excluded). Takt time is:
content.why: Takt = available time / demand = (7.5 × 3600) / 450 = 27,000/450 = 60 s. Takt paces production to demand; cycle time is what the process actually achieves — comparing them drives line balancing.

content.stem: A finishing line runs at 90% availability, 95% performance efficiency, and 98% quality rate. OEE is approximately:
content.why: OEE = A × P × Q = 0.90 × 0.95 × 0.98 = 0.838. OEE multiplies — averaging the three factors (94.3%) is the standard trap. World-class discrete manufacturing is often benchmarked near 85%.

content.stem: A value stream map shows total value-added time of 30 minutes against a production lead time of 600 minutes. Process cycle efficiency is:
content.why: PCE = VA time / total lead time = 30/600 = 5% — typical for unimproved value streams, where most lead time is queue/wait. PCE motivates attacking waiting waste rather than speeding up work steps.

content.stem: On a value stream map, a triangle symbol between two process boxes represents:
content.why: The triangle marks inventory (with quantity/wait noted beneath). Kaizen bursts are starbursts; supermarkets have their own shelf symbol; information flow is drawn with straight/zigzag arrows in the upper band.

content.stem: Operators walk 40 m each cycle to retrieve test rings from a central rack. In the eight-wastes taxonomy this is:
content.why: Motion is unnecessary movement of people; transportation is movement of material/product. The distinction is tested constantly — ask what is moving.

options: Enable later comparison of defect patterns across likely sources of variation
content.stem: A data collection plan's check sheet for surface defects should be stratified by shift, stand, and grade PRIMARILY to:
content.why: Stratification builds analysis capability into collection: recording potential x's (shift, stand, grade) with each defect lets the team compare subgroups later. Unstratified totals hide exactly the contrasts Analyze needs.

content.stem: A team wants a sample size to estimate mean yield strength within ±2 MPa at 95% confidence; historical σ = 10 MPa. The minimum n is approximately:
content.why: n = (zσ/E)² = (1.96×10/2)² = (9.8)² = 96.04 → round up to 97. Always round up; rounding down fails the precision requirement. Halving E would quadruple n — precision is expensive.

content.stem: Time-to-failure data for roller bearings fit a Weibull distribution with shape parameter β = 0.7. This indicates:
content.why: Weibull shape: β<1 → decreasing hazard (infant mortality), β=1 → constant (exponential), β>1 → increasing (wear-out). β=0.7 points to quality/installation defects, not aging — countermeasure is burn-in/screening, not preventive replacement.

options: Constraint exploitation under theory of constraints
Resistance to change requiring stakeholder management
Hoshin misalignment at the annual planning level
content.stem: A plant manager wants to improve tensile-test turnaround but rejects a proposal because it would push cost into the chemistry lab and slow heat release upstream. This objection reflects:
content.why: Optimizing one department at the expense of the whole is suboptimization; recognizing cross-functional interactions before acting is systems thinking. Nothing in the stem indicates emotional resistance or a formal TOC analysis.

options: Time between random arrivals of rush orders
Number of surface defects per coil
Diameter measurements from a stable process
content.stem: Which scenario is correctly matched to the exponential distribution?
content.why: The exponential models time between independent random events (constant hazard) and pairs with the Poisson count of those events. Counts per area → Poisson; proportions → binomial; symmetric measurement noise → normal.

options: Right-skewed with occasional extreme values that distort the mean
content.stem: The median is preferred over the mean as a center measure for cycle-time data primarily because cycle-time distributions are typically:
content.why: Queue-driven cycle times are right-skewed; a few extreme delays drag the mean far above typical experience. The median is robust to such outliers — matching the BOK's guidance on measures of central tendency for skewed data.

options: Sample statistics should be labeled s and x̄; σ and µ denote population parameters
Standard deviation cannot be computed from 25 values
content.stem: A Black Belt computes the mean and standard deviation of 25 heats' Mn content and states 'σ = 0.021.' The correct criticism is:
content.why: Greek letters (µ, σ) denote unknown population parameters; Latin (x̄, s) denote sample statistics that estimate them. The exam tests this notation discipline directly and through inference questions built on it.

options: Reject H₀; there is statistically significant evidence the means differ
Accept H₁ with 97% certainty the difference matters practically

content.stem: A hypothesis test comparing mean yield strength of two suppliers returns p = 0.03 at α = 0.05. The correct conclusion is:

content.stem: A process has an average of 5.50 for the last 20 independent parts and a known historical standard deviation σ = 0.20. Assume individual part values are normally distributed. Use z* = 1.96 to find the 95% prediction interval for the next part produced.

content.stem: A Six Sigma team installs a new drilling-machine guide to reduce hole-location variation. Before improvement, σ = 0.005. Ten independent, normally distributed measurements after the change have s = 0.003. Test H₀: σ = 0.005 versus H₁: σ is less than 0.005 at α = 0.05. Use the lower-tail critical value χ²(0.05, 9) = 3.325.
content.why: The test statistic is χ² = (n − 1)s²/σ₀² = 9(0.003)²/(0.005)² = 3.24. Because 3.24 is below the lower-tail critical value 3.325, reject H₀; the data provide evidence that variation decreased. [VI.B.5]

content.why: z₀ = (0.040 − 0.057)/√[0.057(0.943)/150] = −0.90. Since −0.90 is not below the lower-tail critical value −1.645, do not reject H₀; there is insufficient evidence that the defective rate decreased. [VI.B.5]

content.stem: A new electric vehicle is tested for its maximum range on a single charge. Four vehicles produced the mileage results {260, 252, 254, 254}. content.why: Because the population standard deviation is unknown and n = 4, use a one-sample t test. The sample mean is x̄ = 255 and s = 3.46, so t₀ = (255 − 250)/(3.46/√4) = 2.89. Since 2.89 exceeds 2.353, reject H₀; the data provide evidence that the average range exceeds 250 miles. [VI.B.5]

content.stem: Pieces from five spot-welding stations flow onto a common conveyor belt. An operator chooses five consecutive pieces each hour to test tensile strength. How should the sampling procedure be reconsidered before using an X̄-R chart?

content.stem: Delivering the right level of information, to the right stakeholders, at the right time is part of the:

content.why: Use a c-chart when counting defects per sampling unit with constant sample size. [VIII.A.4]

content.stem: Which of the following subgroup sizes for an X̄-R chart would most likely be used if measurement were costly?
content.why: A subgroup size of 2 minimizes measurement cost while still permitting an X̄-R chart. A subgroup size of 1 requires an individuals and moving-range chart. [VIII.A.4]

content.stem: An R chart is used rather than an S chart because it is:
content.why: An R chart is used rather than an S chart because it is easier to hand-calculate. [VIII.A.4]

content.why: An exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) chart can monitor continuous observations collected one at a time. [VIII.A.4]

content.stem: Which chart is a user-friendly control chart for the operator?
content.why: A median chart is user-friendly for the operator because it does not require any calculation. An odd sample size is used, and all sample values are plotted on the chart. The middle point, or median, is then circled. [VIII.A.4]

content.stem: Why is an R chart generally not recommended for subgroup sizes greater than 9?
content.why: An R chart uses only the subgroup extremes, so it is sensitive to outliers and discards increasingly more information as subgroup size grows. For subgroup sizes greater than 9, an S chart is generally preferred. [VIII.A.4]

cases in which there are few opportunities for nonconformities to occur.

content.why: A fraction nonconforming chart is frequently converted to a percent nonconforming chart so that employees can understand it better. Percentages are often easier for people to evaluate than decimals or fractions. [VIII.A.4]

content.stem: Which sequence lists the phases of DMADV, a common Design for Six Sigma methodology?
content.why: The DFSS phases are define, measure, analyze, design, and verify (DMADV). [IX.A]

content.stem: Which of the following forms of communication can be best used to acknowledge a key milestone?
content.why: Announcements, whether formal or informal, are communications used to acknowledge a key milestone. [II.A]

to design new products and processes to meet Six Sigma quality objectives.

content.stem: Which DMAIC phase is not a named phase in DMADV?
content.why: DMADV consists of Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, and Verify. Control is not a named DMADV phase. [IX.A]

DMEDI develops a new design, so no existing-process baseline is available.

confirm that the completed design meets its specified requirements and performs as designed.
confirm that design inputs describe an intended use.
control every change made during design.

content.why: Both DMAIC and DMEDI have a common define phase. [IX.A]

a variable that can be any constraint to the design process.
a Japanese symbol for zero defects.
content.stem: The X in Design for X is:
content.why: The X in Design for X is a variable that can be any constraint to the design process. [IX.B]

content.stem: Which of the following quality tools is used to diagram a process?
content.why: Flowcharts are graphical representations of the steps in a process and are drawn to better understand processes. [V.A.2]

content.stem: Which of the following tools would be the most appropriate for crisis management?
content.why: Contingency planning (also called a plan B) is used for crisis management, business continuity, and asset security. [I.A.4]

content.stem: Which of the following categories in a SWOT analysis are considered external?
content.why: Opportunities and threats are considered external to the company's direct control. Strengths and weaknesses are identified with respect to the internal capabilities of an organization, while opportunities and threats look outside the organization to identify opportunities for the organization and threats to the organization. [I.A.4]

content.stem: Which is a typical business-continuity risk?
content.why: Business-continuity planning addresses disruptions such as loss of key personnel, sudden market changes, labor actions, data loss, or disasters. [I.A.4]

content.stem: In the stakeholder influence–importance matrix used for this project, frontline workers have little formal decision authority, but their process knowledge and adoption are essential. How should they be classified?
content.why: The frontline workers would likely have low organizational influence but high importance to the project’s success because the change directly affects their work and depends on their knowledge and adoption. [II.A]

content.stem: Six Sigma projects can deliver nonfinancial benefits, such as increased customer satisfaction. These benefits are referred to as:

content.stem: Under the guide’s contingency-planning categories, which event is listed specifically under asset security?
content.why: All of the options may be addressed in contingency plans, but product recalls would be addressed in an asset security contingency plan. [I.A.4]

content.stem: Six Sigma projects may deliver soft savings such as:
content.why: Increased customer satisfaction is a soft benefit because it is valuable but is not directly booked as a current cash-flow saving. The other listed outcomes are explicitly monetized hard savings. [I.A.4]

A champion is also known as a sponsor. [I.B.1]

content.stem: Which action is finance specifically responsible for when validating a Six Sigma project's claimed financial benefits?
content.why: Finance validates the assumptions and estimated financial savings claimed for a Six Sigma project. [I.B.1]

has the authority or ability to make changes in the process as required.
content.stem: The term Green Belt is usually associated with an individual who:

content.stem: Which Six Sigma role is called upon to remove roadblocks when implementing change?
content.why: A project champion is an upper-level manager who serves as a sounding board and can work to remove roadblocks that the improvement team encounters. [I.B.1]

retains a regular role while leading smaller improvement efforts as a Green Belt.

content.stem: Which Six Sigma role is involved in giving on-the-spot training, advising team leaders, and helping a team prepare for tollgate meetings?
content.why: The Six Sigma role of coach is involved in giving on-the-spot training, advising team leaders, and helping a team prepare for tollgate meetings. [I.B.1]

content.stem: If a project stakeholder is deemed to have High Influence and Low Importance, what behavior approach should the project leader adopt for this stakeholder?
content.why: A stakeholder with high influence but low importance to project execution is often a senior administrator or finance representative. The recommended approach is to keep the stakeholder informed to prevent opposition or sabotage. [II.A]

owns a process and has authority to make required process changes.
content.stem: The term Master Black Belt is usually associated with an individual who:
content.why: A Master Black Belt is typically assigned full-time to train and mentor Black Belts and align the organization’s improvement-project portfolio with strategy. Master Black Belts may also authorize Green Belt and Black Belt certification. [I.B.1]

content.why: Lewin's three-stage change model is unfreeze, change, and refreeze. [I.B.3]

content.why: A readiness assessment can be used to determine an organization's willingness to change. [I.B.3]

content.stem: Which of the following types of organizational structure is most resistant to change?
content.why: A highly centralized organizational structure tends to resist any change, and fundamental improvements are difficult to achieve. [I.B.2]

content.stem: Which of the following models is the best for identifying stakeholders of a proposed change in a manufacturing process?
content.why: A SIPOC view identifies suppliers, inputs, the process, outputs, and customers, helping the team identify stakeholders affected by a proposed change. [I.B.3]

divide the responsibility and authority equally between management and the workers.

content.why: A stakeholder with low potential for cooperation and high potential to affect the project is classified as nonsupportive. [II.A]

content.why: The benchmarking process follows the cycle of planning, data collection, analysis, and implementation. [II.B]

content.why: Benchmarking may expose confidential or proprietary information. Confidentiality agreements and a code of conduct help control that risk. [II.B]

content.stem: In a balanced scorecard, which perspective addresses shareholder value?
content.why: The financial perspective provides insight into how well goals, objectives, and strategies are contributing to shareholder value and the bottom line. [II.C.1]

content.stem: An organization's net promoter score is positively correlated to which metric?
